issues.legal_issue: A propounded will surrounded by cumulative, material suspicious circumstances that remain unexplained cannot be accepted as genuine merely because its execution was formally supported by attesting-witness evidence.
material_facts: The document was typed on three differently coloured sheets, and the testator’s signatures were placed inconsistently, made with different pens, and absent from two pages that contained typed matter.
The document also contained blank spaces, incorrect or inconsistent property descriptions, mismatched calendar dates, and a recital describing a past event as future.
The explanation for the different pens was found implausible, and the account that the will had been kept in a sealed cover with an incomplete draft did not dispel the doubts.

Although attesting witnesses supported the alleged execution, the Supreme Court found that the combined abnormal features undermined the document’s genuineness and that the testator had not signed it as a genuine will.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to hold that the document was not the genuine will of the testator; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be made by a person with testamentary capacity and executed as required, including placement of the signature so that it appears intended to give effect to the writing as a will. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires examination of at least one available and capable attesting witness to prove execution, but formal proof does not by itself establish genuineness. The propounder bears the initial burden; when real, germane suspicious circumstances arise, that burden becomes heavier and the propounder must remove them with cogent and satisfactory evidence before the will can be accepted. The Court applied H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Smt. Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, and K. Laxmanan v. Thekkayil Padmini.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_a_propounded_wil: A party appealed in a civil proceeding against a decision concerning whether a document was the deceased person's will.
predicates.document_has_cumulative_material_abnorma: The purported will contains multiple unusual features in its pages, signatures, execution, or contents that together cast material doubt on its authenticity.
predicates.suspicious_features_remain_unexplained: The party relying on the purported will did not provide a cogent and satisfactory explanation that removed the material doubts about its execution.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a purported will with multiple material irregularities that remain satisfactorily unexplained, the will is not accepted as genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court should not remand a civil case for retrial when the parties had a full opportunity to present evidence and the record is sufficient to decide the appeal.
material_facts: The parties had adduced the evidence they wished to present at trial, and the appellants did not claim that they had been denied an opportunity to produce particular evidence or that the trial had been vitiated.
The High Court examined the existing evidence and circumstances, reversed the trial court’s conclusion, and had sufficient material to decide whether the purported will was genuine.
A retrial was not necessary to resolve the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not required to remand the case; the Supreme Court rejected the remand argument and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rules 23 and 23A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, remand is appropriate where the relevant conditions are met and, under Rule 23A, a retrial is considered necessary after reversal of a decree. Rule 24 directs the appellate court to determine the case finally when the evidence on record is sufficient. Remand is not routine and should not be used merely to allow a party to fill a lacuna. The Court also considered Mohan Kumar v. State of Madhya Pradesh and distinguished cases in which an opportunity to adduce necessary evidence is required.

rule.if: civil_first_appeal_from_a_trial_decree and appellate_record_sufficient_to_decide and parties_had_full_opportunity_to_present_evidence and not retrial_necessary

predicates.civil_first_appeal_from_a_trial_decree: A party brought a first civil appeal from a decree made after trial.
predicates.appellate_record_sufficient_to_decide: The evidence already on the record was sufficient for the appellate court to determine the dispute.
predicates.parties_had_full_opportunity_to_present_: The parties had an opportunity to present the evidence they wished to rely on at trial.
predicates.retrial_necessary: A new trial was required to enable a fair and complete determination of the dispute.

issues.definition: When a first civil appeal can be decided on a sufficient record after the parties have had a full opportunity to present evidence, and no retrial is needed, remand is not warranted.
